We propose a novel temporal-varying Poisson autoregression (TVPAR) model that captures the time-varying nature of the autoregressive parameters in a Poisson regression framework. The TVPAR model incorporates a time-varying autoregressive component, allowing the autoregressive parameters to change over time, and a time-invariant Poisson regression component, capturing the effects of covariates on the response variable. We develop a Bayesian approach to estimate the TVPAR model using a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm, which allows for efficient estimation of the time-varying autoregressive parameters. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the TVPAR model using simulated data and real-world applications, including modeling the number of COVID-19 cases in the United States and the number of accidents on a highway. The results show that the TVPAR model outperforms traditional Poisson regression and autoregressive models in terms of predictive accuracy and model fit.

Stellar photometry has emerged as a powerful tool for aerosol assessments, offering a unique perspective on the Earth's atmosphere. By analyzing the light scattered by aerosols, stellar photometry can provide valuable insights into aerosol properties, such as size distribution, optical depth, and refractive index. Recent advancements in this field have led to the development of new techniques and instruments, enabling more accurate and detailed aerosol assessments. This paper reviews the recent progress in aerosol assessments using stellar photometry, highlighting the strengths and limitations of this approach. We discuss the current state of the art, including the use of machine learning algorithms and the integration of stellar photometry with other remote sensing techniques. We also explore the potential applications of stellar photometry in aerosol research, including the study of aerosol-climate interactions and the development of aerosol models. Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive overview of the recent advancements in aerosol assessments using stellar photometry and highlights the potential of this technique for advancing our understanding of the Earth's atmosphere.

We present a novel configurational molecular sampling method, dubbed "Sturdy and Effective Configurational Molecular Sampling via Langevin Dynamics" (SECM-SLD), which leverages the advantages of Langevin dynamics to efficiently explore the configurational space of complex molecular systems. By incorporating a novel adaptive thermostat and a modified friction coefficient, SECM-SLD achieves a balance between exploration and exploitation, allowing for the efficient sampling of rare and high-energy configurations. We demonstrate the efficacy of SECM-SLD through a series of benchmark tests, including the calculation of thermodynamic properties and the prediction of phase transitions in various molecular systems. Our results show that SECM-SLD outperforms existing methods in terms of sampling efficiency and accuracy, making it a valuable tool for the study of complex molecular systems.

This study examines the use of human reference information in evaluating the accuracy of automatic image descriptions. The researchers employed a dataset of 1,000 images, each with a corresponding reference description, to assess the performance of various automatic image description models. The results indicate that the models' performance is significantly improved when using human reference information, with a notable increase in accuracy and a reduction in the number of incorrect descriptions. The study also highlights the importance of considering the context and nuances of human language in the development of automatic image description models.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the hadronic spectrum, focusing on the predictions of the constituent quark model (CQM) and the bag model. Our study includes the masses of baryons and mesons, as well as their decay modes and branching ratios. We also discuss the implications of these predictions for the search for new particles at future colliders. Our results are based on a detailed analysis of the quark model and the bag model, including the effects of quark confinement and the role of gluons in the strong interaction. We find that the CQM and the bag model are in good agreement with each other and with experimental data, and we discuss the implications of this agreement for our understanding of the strong interaction. We also present a new method for predicting the masses of baryons and mesons, based on the use of a variational principle. This method allows us to make precise predictions for the masses of particles that have not yet been observed, and we discuss the potential of this method for the discovery of new particles at future colliders.

This paper presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM equivalents for wideband waveforming, which is a technique that combines data and power transfer in a single transmission. The SISO-OFDM equivalent is a single-antenna system that uses orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) to achieve the same performance as a multi-antenna system. The MISO-OFDM equivalent is a multi-antenna system that uses OFDM to achieve the same performance as a wideband waveforming system. The paper shows that the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM equivalents can be used to create extra benefits beyond multiple antennas and multiple carriers, such as increased data transfer rates and improved power transfer efficiency.

We present a comprehensive theory framework for fitting parton distribution functions (PDFs) to experimental data. Our approach is based on a Bayesian inference method, which allows us to incorporate prior knowledge and uncertainties in the fitting process. We develop a novel method for estimating the uncertainties in the fitted PDFs, which is essential for reliable predictions of physical observables. Our framework is designed to be flexible and can be easily adapted to different experimental data sets and theoretical models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to a variety of experimental data sets, including those from the LHC and Tevatron. Our results show that our method provides more accurate and reliable PDFs compared to traditional methods. We also discuss the implications of our results for future PDF fits and the development of new theoretical models.

A linearized framework is developed to model the reaction of a turbulent jet fire to acoustic forcing using an active flame method. The framework is based on the Navier-Stokes equations and the flame surface density transport equation. The acoustic forcing is modeled using a linearized acoustic pressure term, and the flame response is modeled using a linearized flame surface density transport equation. The framework is validated using experimental data from a turbulent jet fire experiment. The results show that the framework can accurately predict the flame response to acoustic forcing, and that the active flame method can be used to model the reaction of a turbulent jet fire to acoustic forcing.

We present a novel approach to nonlocal gravity, focusing on the role of essential tetrads and constitutive connections. By introducing a nonlocality parameter, we derive a modified Einstein-Hilbert action that incorporates the effects of nonlocality. We then explore the implications of this nonlocality on the behavior of gravitational waves and the properties of black holes. Our results demonstrate that nonlocal gravity can lead to distinct predictions for the propagation of gravitational waves and the behavior of black hole horizons. We also discuss the potential observational signatures of nonlocal gravity and the challenges associated with testing these predictions. Our work provides a new perspective on the nature of gravity and its relationship to nonlocality, and highlights the need for further investigation into the properties and implications of nonlocal gravity.

The LHC has been a powerful tool for probing the Standard Model and searching for new physics beyond it. In this paper, we discuss the role of minor systems in the LHC, which are systems that are not part of the main detectors but are still crucial for the operation and analysis of the data. These systems include the LHC's beam instrumentation, the luminosity monitors, the beam position monitors, and the radiation monitoring systems. We review the current status of these systems and discuss their impact on the LHC's performance and the analysis of the data. We also discuss the future plans for these systems and how they will be used in the next run of the LHC.

We investigate the recurrence periods of neutron star X-ray binary transients and the character of the Galactic Centre quiescent X-ray binaries. Our analysis reveals that the recurrence periods of these transients are not random, but rather follow a power-law distribution. We also find that the quiescent X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre are not a homogeneous population, but rather consist of two distinct sub-populations: one with short recurrence periods and another with long recurrence periods. Our results suggest that the quiescent X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre are not a single population, but rather a mixture of different populations with different properties. We also find that the recurrence periods of the quiescent X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre are not correlated with the mass of the companion star, but rather with the mass of the neutron star. Our results have implications for our understanding of the formation and evolution of neutron star X-ray binaries and the character of the Galactic Centre quiescent X-ray binaries.

We present a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithm for the bipartite vertex division problem, which is a fundamental problem in graph theory. The problem involves partitioning the vertices of a bipartite graph into two sets such that the number of edges between the sets is minimized. Our algorithm runs in time O(2^k * n^O(1)), where k is the size of the smaller set and n is the number of vertices in the graph. This improves upon the previous best known algorithm, which had a running time of O(2^k * n^O(k)). We also provide a lower bound of O(2^k * n^O(1)) for the problem, showing that our algorithm is essentially optimal. Our algorithm is based on a novel approach that combines techniques from parameterized complexity and graph theory. We first show that the problem can be reduced to a problem of finding a minimum cut in a flow network, and then use a flow-based approach to solve the problem. We also provide a number of experimental results that demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm in practice. Overall, our results provide a significant improvement over the previous best known algorithm and demonstrate the power of parameterized complexity in solving hard graph problems.

The increasing power consumption of modern CPUs has led to a significant rise in heat generation, which can cause system crashes and reduce overall performance. To address this issue, researchers have proposed various techniques to reduce CPU frequencies, but these methods often result in significant performance degradation. In this paper, we present HyperDegrade, a novel approach that dynamically adjusts CPU frequencies to achieve a balance between performance and power consumption. By leveraging a combination of machine learning and thermal modeling, HyperDegrade can accurately predict the optimal frequency for a given workload and environment, resulting in a significant reduction in power consumption while maintaining acceptable performance. Our experiments demonstrate that HyperDegrade can achieve a 30% reduction in power consumption at a 10% performance loss, making it a promising solution for future CPU design.

We present a novel unknotting procedure for classical and welded links, which we call the "twist-untwist" method. This method is based on the idea of creating a twist in the link and then untwisting it, which allows us to distinguish between the unknot and other knots. We show that this method is effective for unknotting classical links, and we also extend it to welded links, which are links with a fixed embedding in a surface. Our method is simple to implement and can be used to distinguish between the unknot and other knots in both classical and welded links. We also provide a computer implementation of the twist-untwist method and demonstrate its effectiveness on a large number of examples.

This paper presents a novel approach to multi-agent collaboration in standard networks of robots with restricted computation and communication capabilities. The proposed method, called Tactical Multi-Agent Collaboration (TMAC), enables robots to collaborate effectively in complex tasks despite their limited resources. TMAC is based on a decentralized architecture that allows robots to share information and coordinate their actions in real-time. The approach is designed to be scalable and adaptable to different network topologies and task requirements. The paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of TMAC using simulations and real-world experiments, demonstrating its effectiveness in various scenarios. The results show that TMAC outperforms traditional methods in terms of task completion time and robot utilization. The paper also discusses the implications of TMAC for real-world applications, such as search and rescue, environmental monitoring, and manufacturing.

We introduce a new method for representing groups as wreath products, which we call the Cartesian partition method. This method is based on the idea of partitioning the elements of a group into disjoint subsets, called blocks, and then using these blocks to construct a wreath product. We show that this method is equivalent to the standard wreath product construction, but it provides a more intuitive and computationally efficient way of representing groups as wreath products. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by applying it to several examples, including the symmetric group, the alternating group, and the general linear group. Our results show that the Cartesian partition method is a powerful tool for representing groups as wreath products, and it has the potential to be used in a wide range of applications, including group theory, combinatorics, and computer science.

The paper titled "Improving high frequency responsiveness of gravitational wave sensors with sloshing-Sagnac interferometer" discusses the development of a novel gravitational wave sensor that combines the principles of sloshing and Sagnac interferometry to enhance its high-frequency responsiveness. The authors propose a new design that incorporates a sloshing cavity, which is a resonant cavity filled with a fluid that sloshes back and forth in response to gravitational waves. This design is combined with a Sagnac interferometer, which is a type of interferometer that uses the Sagnac effect to measure the phase shift caused by gravitational waves. The authors demonstrate that the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer can achieve a higher sensitivity to high-frequency gravitational waves than traditional gravitational wave sensors, making it a promising tool for detecting and studying these phenomena. The paper presents a detailed analysis of the design and performance of the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, including its sensitivity, noise characteristics, and potential applications in gravitational wave astronomy.

This paper investigates the non-intersecting visibility areas in XL-MIMO stochastic access protocol. The XL-MIMO system is a type of massive MIMO system that uses a large number of antennas to improve the capacity and reliability of wireless communication. The stochastic access protocol is a technique used to manage the access of multiple users to the XL-MIMO system. The non-intersecting visibility areas refer to the areas in which the users can see each other without any interference. The paper presents a mathematical model to analyze the non-intersecting visibility areas in the XL-MIMO stochastic access protocol. The model takes into account the number of antennas, the number of users, and the distance between the users. The paper also presents a simulation study to evaluate the performance of the XL-MIMO stochastic access protocol in terms of the non-intersecting visibility areas. The results show that the XL-MIMO stochastic access protocol can achieve a high degree of non-intersecting visibility areas, which can improve the capacity and reliability of the wireless communication system.

We propose a novel neural text creation model that incorporates residual learning and $n$-gram language models to generate coherent and contextually relevant text. Our model, called Residual $n$-gram Language Model (RnLM), leverages the strengths of both residual learning and $n$-gram language models to improve text quality and diversity. In the training phase, RnLM uses a combination of masked language modeling and next sentence prediction tasks to learn the underlying patterns and relationships in the input text. During inference, RnLM generates text by iteratively predicting the next word based on the context and the learned $n$-gram patterns. Our experiments demonstrate that RnLM outperforms state-of-the-art models in terms of text quality, diversity, and coherence, making it a promising approach for various natural language processing tasks.

We present iOCR, a novel informed optical symbol recognition system for accurately extracting election ballot totals from scanned images. Our approach leverages a combination of deep learning-based symbol recognition and informed post-processing to address the challenges of optical character recognition (OCR) in this domain. We demonstrate the effectiveness of iOCR on a dataset of 1,000 scanned ballot images, achieving a 99.5% accuracy rate in extracting the correct totals. Our results show that iOCR outperforms state-of-the-art OCR systems, and we provide a detailed analysis of the system's performance and limitations.

The paper titled: Comparative land atmospheric circulation patterns in simplified global circulation models: I. from cyclostrophic super-rotation to geostrophic turbulence, discusses the atmospheric circulation patterns in simplified global circulation models. The authors compare the atmospheric circulation patterns in these models, specifically focusing on the transition from cyclostrophic super-rotation to geostrophic turbulence. The study aims to understand the underlying mechanisms driving these transitions and their implications for the Earth's climate system. The authors use a combination of theoretical and numerical approaches to analyze the models and provide insights into the complex interactions between atmospheric circulation patterns and the Earth's climate. The study contributes to the ongoing research in the field of atmospheric science and climate modeling, providing a deeper understanding of the Earth's atmospheric circulation patterns and their role in shaping the climate.

This paper presents a comprehensive survey of the current state of knowledge acquisition in the context of the educator-pupil framework. The educator-pupil framework is a fundamental concept in education, where the educator plays a crucial role in guiding the pupil's learning process. The paper focuses on the knowledge acquisition process, which is a critical aspect of education. It discusses various aspects of knowledge acquisition, including the role of the educator, the pupil's learning style, and the impact of technology on the learning process. The paper also explores the challenges and limitations of knowledge acquisition in the educator-pupil framework, such as the need for personalized learning, the role of feedback, and the impact of cognitive biases. The paper concludes by highlighting the importance of understanding the knowledge acquisition process in the educator-pupil framework and the need for further research in this area.

We introduce a novel function depiction, called the "brief function," that enables faster exact computation of the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate and constrained optimization in graphical models. The brief function is a compact representation of the model's potential function, which can be computed in linear time. We show that the brief function can be used to efficiently compute the MAP estimate and solve constrained optimization problems in graphical models. Our results demonstrate that the brief function can significantly improve the computational efficiency of exact inference and optimization in graphical models, making it a valuable tool for a wide range of applications.

We introduce the Racah algebra, a new algebraic structure that generalizes the Racah-Wigner algebra. We then study the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ of the $n$-fold tensor product of the special linear Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ with itself, and show that it is isomorphic to the Racah algebra. We also compute the Hilbert-Poincaré series of $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, which is a generating function that encodes information about the dimensions of its irreducible representations. Our results provide new insights into the representation theory of the Racah algebra and the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$.

We propose a new method for paired-permutation examination of structured test statistics, which we call Precise Paired-Permutation Examination (PPE). PPE is designed to efficiently and accurately examine the distribution of test statistics under the null hypothesis, even when the test statistic is structured and the number of permutations is large. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PPE through a series of simulations and real-data applications, showing that it outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. Our results highlight the importance of considering the structure of the test statistic when performing paired-permutation examinations, and we provide a practical guide for implementing PPE in a variety of statistical contexts.

We investigate the triangular flow $v_3$ in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions using a multiphase transport framework. The framework incorporates both the hadronic and partonic phases, allowing for a comprehensive description of the system's evolution. We find that the $v_3$ values are sensitive to the initial conditions, particularly the eccentricity of the participant plane. The framework's ability to reproduce the experimental data is improved when the initial conditions are adjusted to match the observed $v_3$ values. The results suggest that the triangular flow is a valuable tool for understanding the system's initial conditions and the interplay between the hadronic and partonic phases.

This paper presents a novel approach to the problem of sensor administration, specifically the task of detecting and isolating faulty sensors in a network. The proposed method, called the PMBM filter, utilizes a partially grid-oriented birth model to identify and eliminate faulty sensors. The PMBM filter is a type of probabilistic data association filter that uses a grid-based approach to estimate the state of the sensors. The partially grid-oriented birth model is used to model the birth process of new sensors, which is essential for the PMBM filter to function correctly. The proposed method is evaluated using a simulation study, which demonstrates its effectiveness in detecting and isolating faulty sensors. The results show that the PMBM filter outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and robustness. The proposed method has the potential to be applied in various fields, including sensor networks, robotics, and computer vision.

In this study, we propose a novel approach to soccer match analysis using deep reinforcement learning. Our method focuses on identifying critical scenarios in soccer matches and developing enhanced strategies to improve team performance. We utilize a combination of computer vision and natural language processing techniques to analyze match data and identify key events. Our deep reinforcement learning model is trained on a large dataset of soccer matches, allowing it to learn optimal strategies for different scenarios. We evaluate our approach using a range of metrics, including match outcome, possession, and goal-scoring opportunities. Our results show that our approach can improve team performance in critical scenarios, leading to better match outcomes. We also provide a detailed analysis of the strategies learned by our model, highlighting the importance of factors such as possession, passing accuracy, and goal-scoring opportunities. Our study contributes to the development of more effective strategies for soccer teams and provides a framework for analyzing and improving team performance in critical scenarios.

This paper presents a novel approach to control a single-point laser Doppler velocimetry (LDV) system for gathering 2D measurements. The system is controlled remotely using a computer, allowing for precise positioning and measurement of velocity fields in various environments. The control system consists of a computer, a motorized stage, and a single-point LDV system. The motorized stage is controlled using a computer program that allows for precise positioning and movement of the LDV system. The LDV system is used to measure the velocity of particles in a fluid, and the data is collected and analyzed using a computer program. The results show that the system can accurately measure velocity fields in various environments, including turbulent flows and flows with complex geometries. The system is also shown to be capable of measuring velocity fields in real-time, allowing for the analysis of dynamic systems. The paper presents a novel approach to controlling a single-point LDV system for gathering 2D measurements, and demonstrates the potential of this system for a wide range of applications, including fluid dynamics, aerodynamics, and biomedical engineering.

We consider the Klein--Gordon equation linked to an anharmonic oscillator, which is a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a specific potential. We study the spectral and orbital stability of the ground state of this equation, which is a standing wave solution. Our analysis is based on the use of the virial identity and the concentration-compactness principle. We show that the ground state is spectrally stable, meaning that any small perturbation of the ground state will not lead to the creation of new solutions with lower energy. We also show that the ground state is orbitally stable, meaning that any small perturbation of the ground state will not lead to the creation of new solutions with lower energy, even if the perturbation is not small in the sense of the energy norm. Our results are based on the use of the virial identity and the concentration-compactness principle, and they provide a complete characterization of the spectral and orbital stability of the ground state of the Klein--Gordon equation linked to an anharmonic oscillator.

We investigate the possibility of observing axion-like particles (ALPs) in $B$ decays at the Belle II experiment. We consider the process $B^+ \to K^+ a$, where $a$ is an ALP, and the subsequent decay $a \to \gamma \gamma$. We find that the Belle II experiment can potentially observe this process, and we provide a detailed analysis of the expected sensitivity. We also discuss the implications of our results for the search for ALPs in $B$ decays at Belle II.

This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the performance of various contextualized language frameworks in identifying semantic change. The study compares the effectiveness of BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT in capturing semantic shifts in word meanings. The results show that while these frameworks exhibit strong performance in certain tasks, they struggle with identifying subtle semantic changes. The study highlights the importance of considering the nuances of semantic change and the limitations of current contextualized language frameworks. The findings suggest that a more nuanced approach to semantic change identification is necessary, one that takes into account the complexities of language and the context in which words are used.

We investigate the possibility of ultralight bosons with masses in the range of 10^-22 eV to 10^-20 eV, which could be produced via superradiance in massive quasars. We find that the observed spins of these quasars are consistent with the presence of such bosons, and that the boson mass is likely to be in the range of 10^-21 eV to 10^-20 eV. We also find that the boson mass is likely to be in the range of 10^-21 eV to 10^-20 eV, and that the boson spin is likely to be 1/2. Our results suggest that ultralight bosons could be produced via superradiance in massive quasars, and that these bosons could have a significant impact on our understanding of the universe.

We present a novel approach to study the driven quantum harmonic oscillator using the path integral technique and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. The path integral formulation of quantum mechanics is used to represent the time-evolution of the system, and the MCMC method is employed to efficiently sample the high-dimensional path space. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by calculating the time-dependent expectation values of the position and momentum operators for a driven quantum harmonic oscillator. Our results show excellent agreement with exact analytical solutions and provide a powerful tool for studying the dynamics of driven quantum systems. The MCMC method allows for the efficient sampling of the path space, making it possible to study systems with large time-evolution times and high-frequency driving. We also discuss the potential applications of our approach to study other driven quantum systems and the limitations of the method.

We present a quantum relational Hoare calculus with expectations, which is a formal system for reasoning about the correctness of quantum programs. The calculus is based on a relational semantics that captures the probabilistic nature of quantum computation. We define a new notion of expectation, which is a generalization of the classical notion of expectation, and use it to define a new notion of satisfaction for quantum programs. We show that the calculus is sound and complete, and that it can be used to reason about the correctness of quantum programs in a compositional way. We also show that the calculus can be used to reason about the correctness of quantum programs in the presence of noise and errors. Finally, we demonstrate the practicality of the calculus by applying it to a number of examples, including a quantum algorithm for solving the Deutsch-Jozsa problem and a quantum algorithm for solving the Bernstein-Vazirani problem.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the bias in inferred measurements of the solar vector magnetic field (VMF) data, which is a critical component in understanding the solar dynamo and its impact on space weather. Our study reveals that the bias in VMF data is not only present but also varies significantly across different solar cycles and locations on the Sun. We identify the primary sources of bias, including the limitations of the inversion algorithms, the quality of the input data, and the assumptions made during the inversion process. To alleviate the bias, we propose a novel approach that combines multiple inversion algorithms and incorporates a machine learning-based correction technique. Our results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly reduce the bias in VMF data, leading to more accurate and reliable measurements. We also provide a comprehensive evaluation of the performance of the proposed approach, including its sensitivity to different input parameters and its ability to capture the complex dynamics of the solar magnetic field. Our study provides new insights into the bias in VMF data and offers a practical solution for mitigating its effects, which is essential for advancing our understanding of the solar dynamo and its impact on space weather.

We investigate the Boolean structures of involutions, which are endomorphisms of a vector space that satisfy the condition $f^2 = \mathrm{id}$. We show that the Boolean structure of an involution is determined by its rank, and we classify the involutions of a given rank. We also study the involutions of a vector space over a field of characteristic 2, and we show that they are closely related to the symplectic forms on the space. Our results have implications for the study of quadratic forms and the geometry of vector spaces.

In this paper, we investigate the properties of timelike Bertrand curves in semi-Riemannian space. We first recall the definition of Bertrand curves and their relationship with the Frenet frame. We then derive the Frenet-Serret formulas for timelike Bertrand curves in semi-Riemannian space and analyze their properties. We also investigate the relationship between timelike Bertrand curves and the curvature of the ambient space. Our results provide new insights into the geometry of timelike Bertrand curves and their applications in physics and engineering.

This study examines the impact of modifying loss functions on the performance of deep learning models in classification tasks. The researchers investigate the effects of different loss function modifications, including the use of focal loss, label smoothing, and class-balanced loss, on the accuracy and robustness of deep learning models. The study also explores the relationship between loss function modifications and the model's ability to handle class imbalance and outliers. The results of the study suggest that modifying the loss function can significantly improve the performance of deep learning models in classification tasks, particularly when dealing with class imbalance and outliers. The study also highlights the importance of carefully selecting the loss function and its modifications to achieve optimal performance.

ATOMIC is a comprehensive knowledge graph that captures a wide range of common-sense knowledge, including cause-and-effect relationships, physical interactions, and social behaviors. The graph contains over 20 million edges and 1.5 million entities, making it one of the largest and most diverse knowledge graphs available. ATOMIC is designed to support a variety of applications, including question answering, text generation, and decision-making. The relations are used to describe a wide range of phenomena, from physical interactions (e.g., "The ball is on the table") to social behaviors (e.g., "The person is happy"). This paper proposes a novel video forecasting approach that leverages a dual representation to predict future frames. The proposed method, called Dual Representation Video Forecasting (DRVF), consists of two sub-networks: a spatial-temporal network and a temporal-spatial network. The spatial-temporal network focuses on capturing the spatial and temporal relationships between frames, while the temporal-spatial network emphasizes the temporal and spatial relationships between frames. The two sub-networks are trained simultaneously, and their outputs are combined to generate the final prediction. The proposed method is evaluated on several benchmark datasets and achieves state-of-the-art performance. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the dual representation in video forecasting.

The proposed method involves the use of a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract features from the heart sound signals, which are then used to classify the sounds into different categories. The CNN is trained on a dataset of heart sound signals that have been contaminated with additive noise, and the model is able to learn the patterns and features of the signals that are relevant for classification. The subthermal stimulation of the C{\sc i} lines in the molecular gas reservoirs of galaxies is a phenomenon that has garnered significant attention in recent years. This process, which occurs when the C{\sc i} lines are excited by the turbulent motion of the gas, has been found to be a crucial component of the molecular gas cycle in galaxies. The subthermal stimulation of the C{\sc i} lines is important because it allows for the efficient transfer of energy from the turbulent motion of the gas to the C{\sc i} lines, which in turn can be used to heat the gas and drive star formation. This process is particularly relevant in the context of galaxy evolution, where the molecular gas reservoir is a key component of the star formation process. The subthermal stimulation of the C{\sc i} lines is also potentially useful for understanding the properties of the molecular gas reservoir in galaxies, as it can provide insights into the physical conditions of the gas and the processes that govern its evolution.

We introduce a new stochastic process, the ASEP velocity process, which is a continuous-time Markov process that describes the evolution of the velocity of particles in the asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP). The ASEP velocity process is a natural extension of the ASEP, where the velocity of each particle is a random variable that evolves according to a specific dynamics. We derive the master equation for the ASEP velocity process and show that it can be solved exactly using a combination of the Bethe ansatz and the matrix product ansatz. We also derive the hydrodynamic limit of the ASEP velocity process and show that it converges to a deterministic partial differential equation. Our results provide new insights into the behavior of the ASEP and its relation to other stochastic processes, such as the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation.

The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the importance of mathematical modelling in understanding and predicting the spread of infectious diseases. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive overview of the various mathematical frameworks used to model outbreaks, including compartmental models, network models, and agent-based models. We discuss the strengths and limitations of each approach and highlight their applications in the current SARS-CoV-2 epidemic. We also examine the role of data in informing model development and the challenges of integrating model outputs with policy decisions. Our analysis underscores the need for a multidisciplinary approach to modelling outbreaks, combining mathematical techniques with epidemiological expertise and data analysis. By highlighting the potential and limitations of different modelling frameworks, we aim to inform the development of more effective models for predicting and mitigating the spread of infectious diseases.

The relationship between the mass of the central supermassive black hole (M*) and the star formation rate (SFR) of a galaxy is a fundamental aspect of galaxy evolution. However, this connection is observed to turn over at high masses, with the SFR decreasing as M* increases. This phenomenon is not well understood and has been the subject of much debate. Recent studies have suggested that the presence of a bulge in the galaxy may play a key role in this turnover. Bulges are thought to be the result of galaxy mergers and are often associated with high M* and low SFR. In this paper, we investigate the relationship between M*, SFR, and bulge mass in a sample of galaxies. We find that the turnover in the M*-SFR connection is indeed associated with the presence of a bulge, and that the bulge mass is a key driver of this turnover. We also find that the bulge mass is correlated with the M* of the galaxy, suggesting that the bulge plays a key role in regulating the growth of the central black hole. Our results have important implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution and the role of black holes in shaping the properties of galaxies.

We propose a novel approach to cross-lingual sentiment analysis by leveraging a multi-task learning framework. Our method, called Multi-Task Training for Cross-Linguistic Sentiment Assessment (MTCSA), combines the tasks of sentiment classification and cross-lingual text classification to improve the performance of sentiment analysis in low-resource languages. We evaluate our approach on a dataset of 10 languages and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in sentiment classification and cross-lingual text classification. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of MTCSA in improving the performance of sentiment analysis in low-resource languages and provide insights into the importance of task combination in cross-lingual learning.

The paper titled "Spinning up the Surface: Proof for Planetary Ingestion or Unexpected Angular Momentum Transfer?" discusses the possibility of planetary ingestion or unexpected angular momentum transfer in the context of planetary formation and evolution. The authors present a theoretical framework to explain the observed rapid spin-up of the surface of the planet 55 Cancri e, which is thought to be caused by the ingestion of a smaller planet or the transfer of angular momentum from a companion star. The paper provides a detailed analysis of the possible mechanisms and their implications for our understanding of planetary formation and evolution.

This paper proposes a novel approach to identifying false news by leveraging multimodal information and meta-learning. The proposed method, called Meta Neural Process Networks (MNP), combines the strengths of neural process networks and meta-learning to effectively capture the underlying patterns in multimodal data. MNP is trained on a dataset of news articles, images, and videos, and is able to adapt to new, unseen data by learning a set of meta-parameters that can be used to generate a new model for each task. The proposed method is evaluated on a dataset of real-world news articles and is shown to outperform state-of-the-art methods in identifying false news. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of MNP in capturing the underlying patterns in multimodal data and its ability to adapt to new, unseen data.

This paper presents a novel approach to constructing polyphase Golay complementary sets, which are crucial in the design of efficient filter banks and modulation schemes. The authors introduce a new method for creating these sets, leveraging the properties of Golay sequences and the concept of polyphase components. By applying this method, they demonstrate the construction of polyphase Golay complementary sets with improved properties, including increased symmetry and reduced computational complexity. The results are validated through simulations and comparisons with existing methods, highlighting the potential of this approach in various applications, such as filter bank design and modulation analysis.

This paper presents a novel approach to generating realistic cerebral lesions using a progressive adversarial variational auto-encoder (PAVAE). The proposed method leverages a hierarchical structure to progressively refine the representation of the input image, allowing for the generation of high-quality lesions that are indistinguishable from real ones. The PAVAE model consists of multiple stages, each of which refines the representation of the input image using a combination of adversarial and variational learning objectives. The model is trained on a large dataset of cerebral lesions and is able to generate lesions with varying sizes, shapes, and intensities. The generated lesions are evaluated using a range of metrics, including the Dice similarity coefficient, the Hausdorff distance, and the peak signal-to-noise ratio. The results show that the PAVAE model is able to generate high-quality lesions that are comparable to real ones, and outperforms existing methods in terms of lesion similarity and realism. The proposed method has the potential to be used in a range of applications, including medical imaging, computer vision, and data augmentation.

This paper presents a unified structure for feature extraction based on comparative learning, which is a novel approach to feature extraction that leverages the power of comparative learning to extract features from data. The proposed structure consists of a comparative learning module, a feature extraction module, and a feature selection module. The comparative learning module is designed to learn the differences between the input data and a set of reference data, while the feature extraction module is responsible for extracting features from the output of the comparative learning module. The feature selection module is used to select the most relevant features from the extracted features. The proposed structure is evaluated on several benchmark datasets and is shown to outperform state-of-the-art feature extraction methods. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed structure in extracting features that are relevant to the task at hand.

We present ABILITY, a novel framework for integrating structured knowledge into large language models. Our approach leverages a combination of knowledge graph embeddings and a novel attention mechanism to effectively incorporate knowledge into the model's decision-making process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ABILITY on a range of tasks, including question answering, natural language inference, and text classification. Our results show that ABILITY outperforms state-of-the-art models on several benchmarks, and we provide a detailed analysis of its strengths and limitations.

We investigate the shadow thermodynamics of non-linear charged AdS black holes, which are solutions to the Einstein-Maxwell theory with a non-linear electrodynamics source. We find that the shadow radius of these black holes is a function of the charge and the non-linear parameter, and that the shadow radius is larger than that of the Reissner-Nordström black hole. We also find that the shadow radius is a monotonically increasing function of the charge and the non-linear parameter. We then investigate the thermodynamics of these black holes and find that the temperature and entropy are functions of the charge and the non-linear parameter. We also find that the temperature and entropy are monotonically increasing functions of the charge and the non-linear parameter. We then investigate the shadow thermodynamics of these black holes and find that the shadow radius is a function of the temperature and entropy. We also find that the shadow radius is a monotonically increasing function of the temperature and entropy. Our results provide new insights into the shadow thermodynamics of non-linear charged AdS black holes and have implications for the study of black hole physics.

We investigate the dynamics of entanglement and synchronization in a system of two coupled harmonic oscillators. The system is described by a two-mode squeezed state, which is a common model for entangled states. We use the tomographic representation of the system's density matrix to analyze the dynamics of entanglement and synchronization. The tomogram is a two-dimensional representation of the density matrix, which allows us to visualize the dynamics of the system. We find that the entanglement between the two oscillators increases as the system evolves, and that the synchronization between the oscillators also increases. We also find that the entanglement and synchronization are correlated, and that the entanglement is a necessary condition for synchronization. Our results provide new insights into the dynamics of entanglement and synchronization in coupled harmonic oscillators, and have implications for the study of quantum systems and quantum information processing.

We report the observation of the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay and evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay, both of which are the first observed $B^0_s$ decays to a charmed meson and a neutral kaon. The results are based on a sample of $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV collected by the LHCb experiment, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of $9$ fb$^{-1}$. The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay is observed with a significance of $5.4\sigma$, while the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay is observed with a significance of $3.4\sigma$. The branching fractions are measured to be $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L)=(1.15\pm0.24\pm0.07)\times10^{-4}$ and $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L)=(1.35\pm0.35\pm0.09)\times10^{-4}$, where the first uncertainty is statistical and the second is systematic. The results are consistent with the predictions of the Standard Model.

We present a method for constructing the lattice of submodules of a multiplicity-free module from partial data. This method is based on the concept of a "partial submodule" and involves a series of steps to iteratively refine the partial submodule until it is a submodule of the original module. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method using several examples, including the representation of the symmetric group S_5 and the representation of the general linear group GL_2(F_2). Our results show that this method can be used to construct the lattice of submodules of a multiplicity-free module from partial data, and that it can be used to identify the submodules of the module.

In this paper, we investigate Biharmonic hypersurfaces in the Euclidean space, focusing on the repetitive operators. Biharmonic hypersurfaces are a class of submanifolds that satisfy a specific partial differential equation, which is a generalization of the harmonic map equation. The repetitive operators are a set of differential operators that are used to study the properties of these hypersurfaces. We derive the necessary and sufficient conditions for a hypersurface to be Biharmonic, and we show that these conditions can be expressed in terms of the repetitive operators. We also provide examples of Biharmonic hypersurfaces that satisfy these conditions, and we discuss the implications of our results for the study of Biharmonic hypersurfaces in the Euclidean space. Our work provides new insights into the properties of Biharmonic hypersurfaces and sheds light on the relationship between the repetitive operators and the Biharmonic equation.

We introduce the concept of p/q-identifiable sets, which are sets of points in R^d that can be distinguished from each other by a finite number of p/q-summable functions. We show that p/q-identifiable sets are closed under finite unions and intersections, and that they are preserved under homeomorphisms. We also show that p/q-identifiable sets are dense in R^d, and that they have the Baire property. We provide several examples of p/q-identifiable sets, including the set of rational numbers, the set of algebraic numbers, and the set of points with rational coordinates. We also show that the set of p/q-identifiable sets is a sigma-algebra, and that it is generated by the set of rational numbers. Finally, we discuss some open problems related to p/q-identifiable sets, including the question of whether p/q-identifiable sets are closed under countable unions.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate, focusing on the form of the decay rate function. We employ a model-independent approach, utilizing the heavy quark effective theory (HQET) and the operator product expansion (OPE) to describe the decay process. Our analysis is based on a set of differential decay rate functions, each corresponding to a specific form of the decay rate. We use a combination of experimental data from the LHCb collaboration and theoretical calculations to constrain the parameters of the decay rate functions. Our results indicate that the data are consistent with the Standard Model predictions, and we obtain constraints on the parameters of the decay rate functions. We also discuss the implications of our results for the search for new physics in the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ decay.

The unrolling of an adhesive tape is a common phenomenon that produces a characteristic crackling sound. This sound is often perceived as random and chaotic, but recent studies have revealed that it may be more ordered than initially thought. Researchers have discovered that the crackling sound produced by the unrolling of an adhesive tape exhibits a hidden pattern, which is not immediately apparent to the human ear. This pattern is characterized by a specific sequence of sounds, which repeat in a predictable manner. The researchers used a combination of mathematical modeling and experimental techniques to analyze the sound produced by the tape unrolling. They found that the sound can be described by a simple mathematical equation, which captures the underlying order of the sequence. The study provides new insights into the physics of the unrolling process and challenges the traditional view of the crackling sound as a random phenomenon. The findings have implications for our understanding of complex systems and the role of hidden patterns in shaping their behavior.

In this paper, we resolve two long-standing issues raised by Karl Menger in his 1928 paper on angle spaces. The first issue concerns the definition of an angle space, which Menger initially defined as a set of points with a ternary relation. However, he later realized that this definition is not sufficient to ensure the existence of a unique angle between any two distinct points. We show that the definition of an angle space can be modified to include a ternary relation that satisfies a certain condition, which we call the "angle condition." This condition ensures that the angle between any two distinct points is unique. The second issue concerns the existence of a metric on an angle space. Menger showed that an angle space can be equipped with a metric, but he did not provide a clear construction of the metric. We provide a construction of a metric on an angle space that satisfies certain properties, including the angle condition. Our construction is based on the idea of using the angle between two points to define a distance between them. We show that the resulting metric is well-defined and satisfies the properties of a metric. Our results resolve the two issues raised by Menger and provide a more complete understanding of angle spaces.

We propose a novel point cloud smoothing method called Transformation-Unique Smoothing (TPC) that leverages the unique properties of point cloud structures to achieve state-of-the-art results. Unlike traditional smoothing methods that rely on geometric or topological features, TPC focuses on the transformation invariance of point cloud structures, which allows it to preserve the underlying structure while removing noise. Our method consists of two stages: the first stage involves a novel transformation-invariant feature extraction process that captures the structural information of the point cloud, and the second stage involves a smoothing process that leverages the extracted features to remove noise while preserving the underlying structure. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TPC through extensive experiments on various point cloud datasets, including synthetic and real-world data, and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art smoothing methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

We introduce a geometric framework for program evaluation, which provides a unified and flexible approach to evaluating the performance of programs. Our framework is based on the concept of a program as a mapping from input to output, and we represent this mapping as a function on a geometric space. We define a notion of distance between programs based on the difference in their output distributions, and we show that this distance can be computed using a variety of metrics, including the Wasserstein distance and the total variation distance. We also introduce a notion of a "good" program, which is a program that is close to the optimal program in terms of the distance metric. We provide a method for computing the distance between a program and the optimal program, and we show that this method can be used to evaluate the performance of a program. Our framework has several advantages over existing methods for program evaluation, including its flexibility, scalability, and interpretability. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework using a variety of examples, including a simple linear regression model and a more complex neural network.

We establish a new method for computing the Serre weights of a residual representation of the Galois group of a number field, using the theory of Kummer extensions. This method is particularly effective for GL_2 representations, and we use it to compute the Serre weights for a large class of such representations. Our method is based on the idea of using the Kummer theory to compute the weights of the residual representation, and then using the theory of Serre weights to compute the weights of the original representation. We also establish a new criterion for determining whether a representation is of finite slope, and use this criterion to show that many of the representations we consider are of finite slope. Our results have implications for the study of the arithmetic of elliptic curves and modular forms, and we discuss some of these implications in the introduction.

This paper presents a novel approach to detecting damage in self-sensing composites using electrical impedance tomography (EIT) and genetic algorithms. The proposed method involves embedding conductive fibers into the composite material, which enables the measurement of electrical impedance changes in response to damage. The EIT system is used to reconstruct the impedance distribution within the composite, allowing for the identification of damaged regions. A genetic algorithm is employed to optimize the reconstruction process, ensuring accurate damage detection. The proposed method is validated through experiments on composite specimens subjected to various loading conditions, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting damage. The results show that the proposed method can accurately identify damaged regions, even in cases where the damage is not visible to the naked eye. The study highlights the potential of EIT and genetic algorithms in developing advanced damage detection systems for self-sensing composites.

The paper titled: The Application of Geometric Measures in the Tensor Representation of a Euclidean Space, discusses the application of geometric measures in the tensor representation of a Euclidean space. The authors explore the use of geometric measures, such as the Hausdorff dimension and the packing dimension, to analyze the properties of tensors in a Euclidean space. They demonstrate how these measures can be used to classify tensors based on their geometric properties and provide a new framework for understanding the structure of tensors in a Euclidean space. The authors also discuss the implications of their results for various fields, including geometry, topology, and physics.

We study the structure of right-angled Artin groups, focusing on the properties of their right-angled Artin subgroups. We introduce the concept of a "divisor" of a right-angled Artin group, which is a right-angled Artin subgroup that is maximal with respect to the property of being a divisor. We show that every right-angled Artin group has a unique divisor, and that this divisor is a right-angled Artin subgroup. We also show that the divisor of a right-angled Artin group is a characteristic subgroup, and that it is a normal subgroup if and only if the group is a right-angled Artin group of type (2, 2). We provide several examples of right-angled Artin groups and their divisors, and we discuss the implications of our results for the study of right-angled Artin groups.

This paper presents a novel approach to rapidly invert matrices of elevated order using a combination of techniques. The proposed method leverages the power of GPU acceleration to achieve significant speedup over traditional methods. By employing a combination of techniques such as matrix decomposition, iterative refinement, and parallelization, the proposed method is able to invert matrices of elevated order in a fraction of the time required by traditional methods. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in achieving rapid matrix inversion, making it suitable for a wide range of applications.

We consider a distributed contextual linear gambit, where multiple players make decisions based on their private information and the context. The players' payoffs depend on their actions and the actions of other players. We propose a learning algorithm that allows the players to learn their optimal actions without sharing their private information or the context. The algorithm is based on a novel combination of contextual linear regression and a distributed optimization method. We provide a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's convergence and show that it achieves a near-optimal solution in a finite number of iterations. We also provide experimental results that demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness in a variety of scenarios. Our results have implications for the design of distributed decision-making systems, where players need to make decisions based on private information and context.

The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a critical process in the evolution of protoplanetary disks, potentially leading to the formation of giant planets. However, the impact of dust development on VSI remains poorly understood. We investigate the effects of dust development on VSI in the outer zones of protoplanetary disks using a 2D hydrodynamical simulation. Our results show that the growth rate of VSI is significantly reduced in the presence of dust, and the instability is suppressed when the dust-to-gas mass ratio exceeds a critical value. We also find that the suppression of VSI leads to a decrease in the disk's angular momentum transport, which in turn affects the disk's evolution and the formation of giant planets. Our study highlights the importance of considering dust development in the context of VSI and its implications for the formation of giant planets in protoplanetary disks.

We establish a Liouville theorem for Ricci diminutors with constant scalar curvature, which is a generalization of the classical Liouville theorem for Ricci flow. This result is then used to prove a new characterization of the Ricci flow on a closed manifold, which is a generalization of the Perelman's characterization of the Ricci flow. We also provide a new proof of the Liouville theorem for Ricci flow with constant scalar curvature, which is a generalization of the classical Liouville theorem for Ricci flow. The main tool used in the proof is the maximum principle for the Lichnerowicz Laplacian.

We propose a novel approach to dynamic entrance selection, which is a crucial component of multi-branch networks. Our method, called Dynamic Entrances with Global Mean Pooling (DEGMP), leverages global mean pooling to effectively capture the spatial information of the input features. By doing so, DEGMP can accurately identify the most relevant branch for each input sample, leading to improved performance and efficiency. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DEGMP through extensive experiments on various benchmarks, including ImageNet and CIFAR-100. Our results show that DEGMP outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a new state-of-the-art on ImageNet with a ResNet-50 backbone.

We propose a novel federated learning method called Stroll for Education, which leverages a random stroll strategy to adapt to diverse data distributions across clients. Our approach involves a client-server architecture, where the server maintains a global model and the clients maintain local models. The server sends a random stroll of the global model to the clients, who then update their local models using the received stroll and their local data. The updated local models are then sent back to the server, which aggregates the local models to update the global model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Stroll for Education through experiments on several benchmark datasets, showing that it outperforms existing federated learning methods in terms of accuracy and convergence speed.

We propose a simple yet effective consistency regularization technique for semi-supervised medical image segmentation. Our method, dubbed "Awkwardly Simple Consistency Regularization" (ASCR), leverages the idea of consistency between the predictions of a model on the same input but with different augmentations. Unlike existing methods, ASCR does not require any additional network components or hyperparameters, making it easy to implement and integrate into existing pipelines. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ASCR on several medical image segmentation benchmarks, including the ISBI 2013 and 2019 challenges, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art results while being computationally efficient. Our results suggest that ASCR is a valuable addition to the toolkit of semi-supervised medical image segmentation methods.

We investigate the relationship between single-particle entanglement and single-particle steering in the context of bipartite systems. Our analysis reveals that single-particle entanglement is a necessary condition for single-particle steering, but not a sufficient one. We demonstrate that single-particle steering can be achieved without entanglement, and that entanglement does not guarantee steering. Our results have implications for the understanding of nonlocal effects in quantum systems and the development of quantum information processing protocols.

This paper presents a comprehensive literature review on blockchain-supported federated learning frameworks for the Internet of Vehicles (IoV). The IoV is a complex network of interconnected vehicles and infrastructure that relies on data sharing and collaboration to ensure safe and efficient transportation. However, the sharing of sensitive data raises concerns about privacy, security, and data ownership. Federated learning is a distributed machine learning approach that enables multiple parties to collaboratively train a model without sharing their data. Blockchain technology can be used to secure and verify the integrity of the federated learning process. This paper reviews existing blockchain-supported federated learning frameworks for IoV, focusing on their architectures, security mechanisms, and performance evaluation. The review highlights the strengths and limitations of each framework and identifies areas for future research. The findings of this study can inform the development of secure and efficient blockchain-supported federated learning frameworks for IoV applications.

This paper presents a novel method and hardware co-design for energy-saving LSTM networks in video identification tasks. The proposed approach leverages hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition to reduce the computational complexity of LSTM networks. By decomposing the input data into a hierarchical structure, the method achieves a significant reduction in the number of parameters and computations required for the LSTM network. The co-designed hardware architecture incorporates a novel memory access pattern and a hierarchical processing unit to efficiently implement the decomposed LSTM network. The proposed method and hardware co-design achieve a 3.5x reduction in energy consumption and a 2.5x increase in throughput compared to the baseline LSTM network. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in reducing energy consumption and improving performance in video identification tasks.

We investigate the prime decomposition of the iterates of a composition of functions. We show that the prime decomposition of the iterates of a composition of functions can be obtained from the prime decomposition of the original functions. We also provide a formula for the prime decomposition of the iterates of a composition of functions in terms of the prime decomposition of the original functions. Our results have applications in number theory and algebra.

We consider the nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation in the outside of a convex obstacle. We show that the equation has a family of explosion solutions, which are solutions that blow up in finite time. We also show that the explosion solutions are stable under small perturbations. Our results provide new insights into the behavior of solutions to the nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation in the outside of a convex obstacle.

We investigate the positive-characteristic semi-parametric local-uniform deductions of varieties over finitely generated $\mathbb{Q}$-algebras. Our work focuses on the properties of these deductions and their implications for the structure of the underlying varieties. We establish a connection between the semi-parametric local-uniform deductions and the geometric properties of the varieties, providing new insights into the relationship between these concepts. Our results have significant implications for the study of varieties over finitely generated $\mathbb{Q}$-algebras, shedding light on the behavior of these varieties under positive-characteristic semi-parametric local-uniform deductions.

Bayes factors are a powerful tool for comparing the relative evidence of competing models. However, their use in practice is often hindered by the need for careful model specification, the difficulty of computing the evidence, and the challenge of interpreting the results. In this paper, we discuss several strategies for the strong use of Bayes factors, including the use of model averaging, the use of model selection, and the use of model comparison. This paper presents DiscSense, a novel framework for the automated semantic examination of discourse markers. Discourse markers are linguistic elements that facilitate the flow of conversation and convey the speaker's attitude, intention, or relationship with the listener. Despite their importance in human communication, discourse markers have been understudied in the field of natural language processing (NLP). DiscSense addresses this knowledge gap by developing a comprehensive framework for the semantic examination of discourse markers. The framework consists of three main components: (1) a discourse marker identification module, which uses a combination of machine learning and rule-based approaches to identify discourse markers in text; (2) a semantic role labeling module, which uses a graph-based approach to assign semantic roles to discourse markers; and (3) a discourse analysis module, which uses a combination of machine learning and rule-based approaches to analyze the semantic roles assigned to discourse markers. The framework is evaluated on a dataset of 1,000 text samples, and the results show that DiscSense outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and F1-score. The framework has several applications in NLP, including text summarization, sentiment analysis, and dialogue systems.

We present a novel approach to solving extended regular expression inequalities (EREs) using symbolic resolution. Our method, called SRE, is based on a novel representation of regular expressions as Boolean formulas, which enables the application of Boolean satisfiability (SAT) solvers to solve EREs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SRE by comparing it with state-of-the-art tools on a comprehensive benchmark of EREs, showing that SRE outperforms the existing tools in terms of both efficiency and scalability. Our results indicate that SRE is a promising approach for solving EREs, and we believe that it has the potential to become a widely used tool in the field of formal verification.

We study the structure of the operator product expansion (OPE) in the context of the AdS$_{3}$/CFT$_{2}$ correspondence. We focus on the OPE segments, which are the building blocks of the OPE, and examine their properties in the presence of a spin. We find that the OPE segments with spin can be decomposed into a sum of two OPE segments with spin zero, and we derive an expression for the coefficients of this decomposition. We also discuss the implications of our results for the study of the OPE in AdS$_{3}$/CFT$_{2}$ and the computation of correlation functions in the dual CFT.

The development of lobster-eye lenses has been a significant advancement in the field of X-ray optics. These lenses are capable of focusing X-rays onto a detector, allowing for high-resolution imaging. However, their application is limited to a narrow field of view, which restricts their use in certain applications. To address this limitation, a new concept for broad-field X-ray monitoring has been proposed. This concept involves the use of multiple lobster-eye lenses, which are arranged in a specific configuration to achieve a broader field of view. The proposed configuration consists of a series of lenses, each with a different focal length, which are arranged in a hexagonal pattern. This arrangement allows for the collection of X-rays from a larger area, resulting in a broader field of view. The proposed concept has been simulated using ray tracing software, and the results show that it is capable of achieving a field of view of up to 10 times larger than a single lobster-eye lens. The concept also has the potential to be used in a variety of applications, including astronomy, medical imaging, and materials science. Overall, the proposed concept for broad-field X-ray monitoring using multiplexing lobster-eye lenses has the potential to revolutionize the field of X-ray optics and enable new applications that were previously not possible.

The cosmic velocity field is a fundamental component of the large-scale structure of the universe, and its relationship with dark matter halo properties is a topic of ongoing research. Recent studies have shown that the velocity field can be used to infer the mass of dark matter halos, but the underlying physical mechanisms are not yet fully understood. In this paper, we use deep learning techniques to investigate the relationship between the cosmic velocity field and the mass of dark matter halos. Our results show that the velocity field is a powerful predictor of halo mass, and that the relationship between the two is complex and non-linear. We also find that the velocity field is sensitive to the properties of the underlying dark matter distribution, and that it can be used to constrain models of dark matter. Our findings have important implications for our understanding of the large-scale structure of the universe, and highlight the potential of deep learning techniques for analyzing complex astrophysical data.

We report on the use of atomic interferometry to measure local magnetic field alterations with high sensitivity. Our approach leverages the Meissner effect exhibited by superconducting materials, which expel magnetic fields from their interior. By placing a superconducting material near the atomic interferometer, we can create a region with a reduced magnetic field, allowing us to detect even small changes in the local magnetic field. Our results demonstrate the potential of this method for precise measurements of magnetic field alterations, with a sensitivity of 10^-12 T. This technique has applications in various fields, including geophysics, materials science, and quantum metrology.

The Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) states are a type of localized electronic state that arises at the interface between a superconductor and a magnetic impurity. These states are of great interest in the study of superconductivity and its interaction with magnetic materials. In this paper, we develop a relativistic initial principles theory of YSR states, which allows us to accurately describe the electronic structure of these states in a fully relativistic framework. We apply this theory to the case of an Mn adatom and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface, which is a well-studied system in the field of superconductivity. Our results show that the YSR states in this system exhibit a rich and complex behavior, with multiple branches of states that arise from the interaction between the Mn impurities and the Nb superconductor. We also find that the YSR states in this system are highly sensitive to the orientation of the Mn impurities, which can lead to significant changes in the electronic structure of the system. Overall, our results provide new insights into the behavior of YSR states in the presence of magnetic impurities and highlight the importance of relativistic effects in the study of these states.

Skin carcinoma identification based on deep learning and entropy to identify outlier samples. 

Abstract: Skin carcinoma is a common type of skin cancer that can be life-threatening if left untreated. Early detection and diagnosis are crucial for effective treatment and improved patient outcomes. Traditional methods of skin carcinoma diagnosis rely heavily on visual inspection and histopathological examination, which can be time-consuming and prone to human error. In this study, we propose a novel approach to skin carcinoma identification using deep learning and entropy-based outlier detection. Our method involves training a convolutional neural network (CNN) on a large dataset of skin images to learn features that distinguish between normal and cancerous tissues. We then use the entropy of the CNN's output to identify outlier samples that are likely to be misclassified. Our results show that the proposed method achieves high accuracy in identifying skin carcinoma, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) of 0.95. Furthermore, the entropy-based outlier detection method is able to identify 92% of the outlier samples, which are likely to be misclassified. Our study demonstrates the potential of deep learning and entropy-based outlier detection in improving the accuracy and reliability of skin carcinoma identification.

The estimation of vector boson production in high-energy muon collisions is a crucial task in particle physics. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to estimate the vector boson production in high-energy muon collisions. Our method is based on a combination of machine learning algorithms and traditional statistical methods. We use a deep neural network to predict the vector boson production cross-section, and then use a Bayesian approach to estimate the uncertainty of the prediction. We also use a Monte Carlo simulation to validate our results. Our results show that our method is more accurate and efficient than traditional methods, and can be used to estimate the vector boson production in high-energy muon collisions.

This paper explores the intersection of the work of Kurt Gödel, Alfred Tarski, Rudolf Carnap, and John Rosser, four influential logicians who made significant contributions to the development of modern logic. The problem is formulated as an optimization problem, where the objective function is the difference between the calculated and measured acoustic pressures. The optimization variables are the structural parameters, and the constraints are the equations of motion for the structure and the acoustic pressure equations. The problem is solved using a gradient-based optimization algorithm, and the results are compared with the exact solution obtained using the finite element method.
